## Overview

This page documents how we went from the MET Employability Career Match API to
`data/processed/career_market_panel.csv` -- the cleaned, filtered dataset that powers the
[Market Baseline](market_baseline.qmd) page and the rest of this product. Every filtering and
cleaning decision below is anchored to our Step 1 scope: the **Data Analyst -> Data Scientist /
Analytics Engineer** career pathway, inside **NAICS 5182** (Computing Infrastructure Providers,
Data Processing, Web Hosting, and Related Services).

## Industry Filter: NAICS 518, not just 5182

We initially queried the API with `naics=5182` and got only 10 postings back -- far too few to
build a market baseline from. Investigating further, we found the source data tags this same
industry under two different granularities: `518000` (4,299 postings) and `518200` (10
postings), both labeled identically as "Computing Infrastructure Providers, Data Processing, Web
Hosting, and Related Services." Querying the broader `naics=518` catches both, correctly
capturing our full Step 1 industry scope: **4,309 postings**.

## Geographic Filter: US-Only

Our product is scoped around the US labor market (our Step 1 rationale leaned on BLS/FRED
national statistics), so we restricted the dataset to US-based postings.

The `state` field in the source data is inconsistent -- a mix of full state names, abbreviations,
literal "United States," country names, Canadian provinces, European NUTS region codes, and even
city names that leaked into the wrong field. We classified each posting as US or non-US using:

1. A direct match against US state names/abbreviations, or the literal "United States"
2. For blank or `"Remote"` state values, a check of the `city` field for a country/city signal
   (many "Remote" postings actually named a specific country there, e.g. `city: "Lithuania"`)
3. Anything matching a known country name, Canadian province, or NUTS code was excluded

Postings with no resolvable US signal anywhere were **excluded**, not guessed into either
bucket. Result: 4,309 -> **2,469 US postings**, with 1,840 excluded (1,069 confirmed non-US,
771 unresolvable).

## Role Filter: Title Keyword Matching

Per the Step 2 scope rules, we filtered to the subset of postings actually on our career
pathway, using **title-keyword matching** rather than SOC-code-based filtering. We chose
keywords over SOC codes because SOC tags in this dataset are demonstrably unreliable -- see the
[SOC Data Quality](#a-note-on-soc-code-reliability) note below. Title text is the most direct
evidence of what a job actually is.

Keywords used: `data analyst`, `data scientist`, `data engineer`, `business analyst`,
`BI analyst`, `business intelligence analyst`, `analytics engineer`, `ML engineer`,
`machine learning engineer`, `applied scientist`, `data architect` / `database architect`.

This is a deliberately broader set than just "data analyst" and "data scientist" -- it
includes the adjacent roles (Data Engineer, ML Engineer, Data Architect) that make up the
realistic ladder between an entry-level Data Analyst role and a Data Scientist role, matching
our Step 1 pathway framing. Result: 2,469 -> **259 role-matched postings**.

## Deduplication

We found 1 exact duplicate (identical title, company, and state) and removed it, leaving
**258 final rows**.

## Cleaning the Core Variables

### Salary

The API provides separate annual and hourly salary fields. We:

- Annualized hourly rates (`hourly x 2080` hours/year)
- Found and corrected **two rows with values swapped** between the annual and hourly fields in
  the source data (e.g. one row had `42-78` filed as an *annual* salary -- clearly an hourly
  rate; another had `85000-95000` filed as *hourly* -- clearly an annual salary). We corrected
  both using a $1,000 sanity threshold.
- Where both structured fields were blank, we searched the free-text job description for an
  explicit dollar figure (e.g. "Salary: $97,510 - $133,100 per year") as a fallback, recovering
  16 additional rows.
- Final coverage: **89/258 (34%)**. The remaining 169 postings state no salary information
  anywhere, structured or in text -- this is a real market pattern (most postings in this space
  don't disclose pay), not a parsing gap. We manually spot-checked a sample to confirm.

### Experience

No structured "years of experience" field exists in this API tier (the richer `job-facts`
endpoint that would have one is currently empty platform-wide -- a known limitation of the
API, not our pipeline). We parsed minimum years of experience from free text using both digit
patterns ("5+ years") and word-form patterns ("minimum of three years"). Coverage: **131/258
(51%)**; the rest were manually spot-checked and genuinely don't state a requirement.

### Education

Same limitation as experience -- no structured field. We keyword-matched for Bachelor's,
Master's, PhD, and Associate's degree mentions in the free text. Coverage: **45/258 (17%)** --
most postings in this space simply don't state a degree requirement, consistent with a
broader skills-based hiring trend in tech.

### Location

Standardized inconsistent state values (full names, abbreviations, and a handful of city names
that leaked into the state field, e.g. "Francisco" -> California) into a clean state name +
abbreviation. Where no reliable state could be determined, we labeled it `"Unknown"` (42/258,
16%) rather than guess.

### Company Names

A number of postings came through Applicant Tracking Systems where the "company" field was
actually a login-portal subdomain rather than the employer's real name (e.g.
`careers.snowflake.com`, or opaque Oracle Cloud tenant codes like `ecqf.fa.em2.oraclecloud.com`).
We recovered the real employer name where it was legible from the domain, and explicitly
labeled the rest `"Unknown employer (ATS-hosted posting)"` rather than guess. Separately, 19
postings had `"Jobs via Dice"` as the company name -- a job-board aggregator placeholder, not a
real employer -- relabeled `"Unknown employer (job board aggregator listing)"`. In total,
35/258 (14%) have no attributable real employer and are excluded from "top employers" rankings,
though their role/salary/location data is still valid and kept in the dataset.

### A Note on SOC Code Reliability

The source classifier's occupation (SOC) tags are not fully reliable for this dataset. For
example, two postings for "Senior Optical Test Setup Engineer" and "Senior Photonics Test
Engineer" at a hardware company were tagged SOC `27-2011` -- "Actors." Because we filter by
title text rather than SOC code, these misclassifications don't affect which postings make it
into our dataset, but we flag 14/258 rows with implausible SOC tags via the `soc_quality_flag`
column so this field isn't mistaken for ground truth in later analysis.

## Summary

| Stage | Rows | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Raw NAICS 518 pull | 4,309 | All countries, all job types |
| US-only filter | 2,469 | 1,840 excluded (non-US or unresolvable) |
| Role-keyword filter | 259 | 2,210 excluded (not on our career pathway) |
| Deduplication | 258 | 1 exact duplicate removed |

The full column-by-column data dictionary is available in
[`data/processed/data_dictionary.md`](data/processed/data_dictionary.md). The cleaned dataset
itself is at [`data/processed/career_market_panel.csv`](data/processed/career_market_panel.csv).

See the [Market Baseline](market_baseline.qmd) page for the resulting exploratory analysis.
